metadata.file_name: 6. Elouafi. (2025). Uncovering Key Factors of Student Performance in Math_ An Explainable Deep Learning Approach Using TIMSS 2019 Data.pdf
metadata.title: Uncovering Key Factors of Student Performance in Math: An Explainable Deep Learning Approach Using TIMSS 2019 Data

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses TIMSS 2019 international database data and restricts the analytic sample to Moroccan eighth-grade students. The authors describe stratified random sampling at the TIMSS design level and construct a binary target from TIMSS plausible values (PVs), but they do not report applying any student/sampling weights or replicate weights in the machine-learning training/evaluation. They explicitly remove technical variables (including identifiers, weights, and metadata) from the predictive modeling phase, which suggests weights were not used as model inputs; however, the manuscript does not state whether survey weights were used for weighted estimation or evaluation. Because the models are standard classifiers trained on latent features (autoencoder + RF/XGBoost/SVM/DT), the paper does not document a complex-survey-weighted ML procedure, so results should be interpreted as unweighted (or at least not transparently weighted) estimates for the Moroccan eighth-grade population.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The paper constructs a binary target by grouping TIMSS PV tiers (Low vs Intermediate/High/Very High) but does not document how the five PVs were combined into a single classification target (e.g., whether PVs were averaged, treated as multiple observations, or combined via a specific rule). It also does not report any explicit missing-data handling strategy for questionnaire variables after the described variable-exclusion steps (e.g., whether remaining missing values were imputed or cases were removed). Given that TIMSS questionnaire data typically contain item nonresponse, this omission is a reporting gap that limits reproducibility and may affect model calibration and feature importance stability.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used TIMSS 2019 international database and restricted to Morocco (eighth grade / collège; ages ~13–14). Built the modeling dataset from student, teacher, and school questionnaires, starting with 700 variables and removing 41 technical variables (identifiers/weights/metadata/duplicates), excluding 61 variables with 100% missingness (not administered in Morocco), excluding 74 variables with >50% missingness (rarely implemented school policies), discarding 29 redundant variables already captured in alternative formats, and excluding 95 reference variables including plausible values (PVs) from the predictive modeling inputs. Created the binary target from PV tiers by merging Intermediate/High/Very High into one class and keeping Low as the other class to address class imbalance.

main_findings.performance_metrics: SVM (best): Accuracy=0.74, F1=0.73, AUC=0.79. XGBoost: Accuracy=0.73, F1=0.71, AUC=0.76. Random Forest: Accuracy=0.71, F1=0.69, AUC=0.75. Decision Tree: Accuracy=0.65, F1=0.64, AUC=0.68.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS 2019 Grade 8 Mathematics data for Morocco, the study leveraged teacher instructional practices, teacher professional development, and school resource indicators (e.g., explanations, linking to prior knowledge, PD, and library/computers) to predict students’ binary mathematics performance derived from PV tiers, finding that SVM achieved the highest discrimination (AUC=0.79) and balanced classification (F1=0.73). This indicates that strengthening interactive pedagogy and targeted teacher development—alongside improving access to learning resources—may improve the identification of at-risk students and guide more actionable classroom and school interventions, though causality cannot be inferred from predictive SHAP-based feature attribution.

data.outcome_summary: The study analyzes TIMSS 2019 Grade 8 Mathematics data restricted to Morocco (n=8458 students) and constructs a binary target by grouping PV tiers: Low vs Intermediate/High/Very High. After cleaning the questionnaire-derived feature set from 700 variables down to 400 (excluding technical variables, high-missingness items, redundant scores, and PV reference variables), the authors train an autoencoder to compress the 400 inputs into 20 latent dimensions. They then train four classifiers (Random Forest, XGBoost, SVM, Decision Tree) on the latent features and evaluate using accuracy, F1-score, and ROC-AUC. SVM performs best with Accuracy=0.74, F1=0.73, and AUC=0.79, followed by XGBoost (0.73/0.71/AUC=0.76). Interpretability is provided via SHAP on latent dimensions and projection back to original variables, but the paper does not report a transparent PV-combination rule for the binary target nor a missing-data handling method, and SHAP-based importance should not be interpreted as causal effects.
